name: cbmc
why: A bounded model checker that exhaustively explores C programs for assertion violations; a real formal-methods door into proving code wrong.

brief.what_it_is: CBMC is a bounded model checker for C and C++ programs. It takes C or C++ source (the homepage says C89, C99, most of C11/C17 and most compiler extensions from gcc, clang and Visual Studio; the GitHub README adds C23 and SystemC via Scoot) and checks it for memory safety, array bounds, pointer misuse, various undefined-behaviour cases, and user-written assertions. It reports violations it finds, and it can also check C or C++ for I/O equivalence with other languages such as Verilog. The 'executables' list in the package metadata is a family of tools (cbmc, goto-cc, goto-instrument, goto-analyzer, jbmc, and others), and the README points to TOOLS_OVERVIEW.md for what each does. The homepage notes that a Java bytecode variant is called JBMC and that Rust is handled by Kani.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents CBMC as a tool for verifying memory safety and user assertions in real C code, and the README frames it as a way to check C and C++ programs for bugs such as buffer overflows and pointer errors. The homepage's primary reference is 'A Tool for Checking ANSI-C Programs', and the project is credited to research sponsored by SRC, NSF, ONR, NRL, DARPA and ARO, with Daniel Kroening listed as the contact.
brief.how_it_works: CBMC verifies a program by unwinding its loops up to a bound and turning the unwound program into a logical equation. That equation is passed to a decision procedure. By default it uses a built-in solver for bit-vector formulas based on MiniSat, and it can also use external SMT solvers; the homepage recommends Boolector, CVC5 and Z3, which must be installed separately.

brief.install_notes: Windows: download the cbmc-6.8.0-win64.msi installer and run it. It is a command-line binary with no GUI, so run it from the Visual Studio Command Prompt. The GitHub README says the MSI depends on the Visual C++ redistributables, and you need to install vcredist.x64.exe from Microsoft if you don't already have them. Visual Studio Community is recommended. macOS: Homebrew is the easiest route, and you need the Command Line Tools for Xcode installed. Linux: you can use the distribution package, the per-release .deb (which must match your OS version because of libc/libc++ ABI differences), or compile from source following COMPILING.md in the repository. External solvers (Boolector, CVC5, Z3) are optional and must be installed separately. The homepage says they have different licences. The README also mentions a homebrew tap for installing historic versions.
brief.standout: The 'exhaustive' framing in the scout note needs correcting: this is a bounded checker, so it proves properties only up to the loop unwinding bound. It has been around for a long time, with a 2000-era reference paper that still gets many citations. It also covers a wider range than most C checkers, including I/O equivalence against other languages and a family of companion tools for analysing compiled goto programs.
brief.status: Maintained, as far as I can tell. The homepage says CBMC version 6 has been released, with a 6.8.0 binary for Windows and Ubuntu, and Fedora 44 packages 6.8.0. The GitHub README links to a releases page and a CI and coverage setup. I did not find an explicit date for the latest release or commit on the pages I read.
brief.caveats: CBMC is bounded: it only covers loop iterations up to the unwinding limit. Version 6 changed defaults: standard undefined-behaviour checks are on by default (use --no-standard-checks to turn them off), malloc may return NULL by default (use --no-malloc-may-fail), calls to bodiless functions now fail verification, and default verbosity is 6. The homepage lists the licence as BSD 4-clause, and the external solvers have their own licences. The Windows build has no GUI and must be run from the Visual Studio Command Prompt. The homepage says the Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04 binaries are on the project site rather than the standard repositories, since the distro packages are old. The homepage was reachable, and I did not hit any build or runtime problems.
quotes: CBMC is a Bounded Model Checker for C and C++ programs.
The verification is performed by unwinding the loops in the program and passing the resulting equation to a decision procedure.
Releases are tested and for production use.
Develop versions are not recommended for production use.

judge.reason: CBMC turns bounded C/C++ executions into solver queries, making formal verification tangible by finding concrete counterexamples to safety properties and assertions.

entry.title: CBMC
entry.tldr: A bounded model checker for C and C++ that turns your program into a logic equation and searches for inputs that break your assertions.
entry.deeper_look:
CBMC reads C or C++ source and checks it for memory safety, array bounds, pointer misuse, various undefined-behaviour cases, and assertions you write yourself. When it finds a violation, it reports it. It can also check C or C++ for I/O equivalence against other languages such as Verilog.

The method is the interesting part. CBMC unwinds the program's loops up to a fixed bound and turns the result into a logical equation. That equation goes to a decision procedure: by default a built-in bit-vector solver based on MiniSat, or an external SMT solver such as Boolector, CVC5 or Z3. In the project's words: "The verification is performed by unwinding the loops in the program and passing the resulting equation to a decision procedure." A solver answering yes or no replaces a test suite sampling a few inputs.

The word bounded matters. CBMC covers loop iterations only up to the unwinding limit, so a clean result is a proof about that bound, not about every possible run. That is the trade that makes this kind of checking practical on real code.

The package installs a whole family of tools: goto-cc compiles to a goto-program form, goto-instrument and goto-analyzer work on it, and jbmc is the Java bytecode variant. The README points to TOOLS_OVERVIEW.md for what each does. The reference paper, 'A Tool for Checking ANSI-C Programs', dates from around 2000 and is still widely cited. The work was sponsored by SRC, NSF, ONR, NRL, DARPA and ARO.
entry.install:
brew install cbmc
# macOS needs the Xcode Command Line Tools. External solvers (Boolector, CVC5, Z3) are optional and installed separately.

entry.whats_unique: It reaches further than most C checkers: C++, I/O equivalence against languages like Verilog, and a set of companion tools for analysing compiled goto programs. It has also been around for over twenty years.
entry.caveats: Results hold only up to the loop unwinding bound, and version 6 changed defaults: undefined-behaviour checks are on, malloc may return NULL, and calls to bodiless functions fail verification.
